text: PASSAGE (SRC-03-P1): The story of Eklavya is usually told as a lesson in devotion. A tribal boy, refused instruction by the royal teacher Drona, makes a clay image of the master and practises before it until his archery rivals that of the finest prince. When Drona learns of this, he asks for his fee: the boy's right thumb. Eklavya gives it without a murmur, and the tale praises his obedience. Yet many modern readers find the same episode troubling for a different reason. It shows talent that grew without privilege being deliberately cut short so that a favoured pupil might remain unrivalled. Read this way, the story is less about loyalty than about the gatekeeping of skill, and about how institutions can protect rank by denying opportunity. Neither reading is entirely wrong. The epic does not hide the injustice; it records it plainly and leaves the listener uneasy. Perhaps that is its lasting value. A story that only rewarded virtue might be forgotten quickly, but one that makes us ask whether merit was truly honoured keeps returning, generation after generation, as a question rather than an answer. || What is the central theme of the passage?

option_B: Modern readers have completely rejected the traditional reading of the story
option_C: The Eklavya story can be read both as praise of devotion and as a record of talent being denied a fair chance
option_D: Eklavya was the greatest archer of the epic age

subject: Reading Comprehension
text: PASSAGE (SRC-03-P2): Automated systems now help to approve loans, sort job applications and flag suspicious transactions. Their appeal is easy to understand: they work quickly, never tire and apply the same rule to every case. Yet these strengths conceal a weakness. A system trained on past decisions can absorb the biases of those decisions and repeat them at a scale no single clerk could reach. Because its reasoning is often hidden inside layers of calculation, an unfair outcome may go unnoticed for months. For this reason, many experts argue that important decisions should keep a person 'in the loop', someone who can question an output, ask for an explanation and overrule the machine when needed. Oversight of this kind is not a sign of distrust in technology, any more than a co-pilot is a sign of distrust in the pilot. It does, however, carry costs. A reviewer who checks thousands of cases may begin to approve whatever the system suggests, turning supervision into a mere formality. Effective oversight therefore depends on giving reviewers time, training and genuine authority, so that the human check remains a real judgement rather than a signature. || According to the passage, an unfair outcome produced by an automated system may go unnoticed because:
